notes.meaning: Jesus warns that terrible days of suffering are coming upon Jerusalem. Usually, Jewish mothers counted having babies as a great blessing and being childless as a sorrow. In the terrible siege to come, women without children would be spared the heartbreak of watching their little ones starve or die.

The agony in those coming days will be so severe that people will beg for rocks and hills to collapse on top of them. A quick death under falling mountains would seem far better than suffering through the horrors of the city's ruin. Men naturally hide in caves from danger, but here they would rather be crushed than face what is coming.

Jesus uses a well-known saying comparing good people to living, green wood and evil people to dried-up wood. If the Romans carry out such cruelty against Jesus, who is innocent and full of goodness, far worse horrors will fall on a guilty city. Dry wood catches fire quickly, picturing how fast judgment will consume those who reject God.

Roman guards led two actual criminals out to be put to death alongside Jesus. Placing Him with thieves made Him look like a criminal too, adding to His public shame. Yet through it all, Jesus willingly gave Himself up to die rather than being a helpless victim.

The soldiers brought Jesus to the execution site called The Skull, or Calvary, and nailed Him to a wooden cross. They placed Him right between the two criminals, treating Him as the chief offender. In this painful death, He took the curse that sinners deserved upon Himself.

While hanging in pain, Jesus asked His Father to forgive the people who were executing Him. The Roman soldiers did not realize they were crucifying the Son of God, and Jesus lovingly prayed for them instead of seeking revenge. Nearby, the soldiers gambled for His clothes, leaving Him with nothing so that believers could be richly blessed.

The crowds stood staring while the Jewish religious leaders sneered and made fun of Jesus. They told Him to rescue Himself from the cross if He truly was God's chosen Messiah. They did not understand that Jesus had to stay on the cross and refuse to save Himself so that He could save others.

The Roman soldiers also joined in the cruel teasing and offered Jesus cheap sour wine. This cheap wine was what common soldiers drank every day while on guard duty. Some think they were teasing His thirst by holding the cup close and then pulling it away.

The soldiers mocked Jesus' royal claim, telling Him to prove He was the King of the Jews by coming down from the cross. They treated His title as a joke because He looked weak and beaten. True royalty was shown as He silently bore their insults to finish His mission.

A written sign was placed above Jesus' head stating the official legal charge: This is the King of the Jews. Roman rulers wrote such notices so everyone would know why the prisoner was condemned. Without meaning to, the governor published the glorious truth about who Jesus truly is.

One of the dying criminals kept insulting Jesus by demanding that He prove He was the Christ by breaking them all out of death. The man only cared about saving his physical life, not about being rescued from his sins. Even while facing eternity, his heart remained hard and angry toward God.

The other dying criminal spoke up and corrected his partner for mocking Jesus. He warned him that both of them were about to meet God as their Judge and should fear Him. Facing death had softened this man's heart to see his need for mercy.

The second criminal openly admitted that they deserved to die because of their evil crimes. At the same time, he stated that Jesus had done nothing wrong and was completely innocent. True repentance begins when someone honestly confesses their guilt before God.

The penitent thief asked Jesus to remember him when He took up His royal rule. Even while Jesus was dying in shame, this criminal believed that Jesus was a King who would rule beyond death. He did not ask for high honors, but simply trusted Jesus not to forget him.

Jesus gave the dying man an immediate promise that they would be together that very day in paradise, the joyful home of God. The man had no time to do good works, yet Jesus gave him full salvation simply through faith. This shows that no sinner needs to despair of mercy, even at the very end of life.

differ.view: The thief was never baptized and never took communion, showing that a person is saved through faith in Christ alone rather than by ceremonies.
Not receiving baptism does not condemn someone, but despising it does; the thief received the very same promise of the Word that baptism gives.

notes.meaning: Around noon, an unnatural darkness spread over the whole land and lasted until three in the afternoon. This was not a normal sun eclipse, since the moon was full during the Passover festival. The sudden blackness was a miraculous sign of deep sorrow and God's holy judgment on sin.

The light of the sun failed, and the heavy curtain inside the Jerusalem temple tore right down the center. This sacred curtain had kept ordinary people separated from the Most Holy Place where God's presence dwelt. Its tearing showed that Jesus' sacrifice finished the old temple system and opened direct access to God.

Jesus shouted with a strong voice, placing His human soul safely into the hands of His heavenly Father, and then He died. Because He was sinless, death had no power over Him, so He gave up His spirit by His own choice. His dying words show complete trust as He entered heavenly rest.

The Roman officer in charge watched how Jesus died and praised God for what he saw. He declared publicly that Jesus was truly an innocent and righteous man. Even an enemy soldier was led to confess that the Sufferer was blameless.

The crowds who had come out to watch the crucifixion walked home striking their chests in great grief. Striking the chest was an ancient custom showing deep inner fear, guilt, and sorrow. They realized that terrible judgments were coming because an innocent life had been taken.

The close friends of Jesus, along with the devoted women who had traveled with Him from Galilee, watched everything from a distance. They loved Him dearly but could only stand by helplessly in their grief. God kept this small flock safe even in the middle of Christ's enemies.

A council member named Joseph, who lived in Arimathea, was an upright and good man who was eagerly waiting for God's kingdom. Although he belonged to the Jewish high court, he had refused to support their plan to condemn Jesus. His quiet faithfulness showed that not every leader was against the Lord.

Joseph went directly to the Roman governor Pilate and asked permission to take Jesus' body for burial. The Romans usually left executed men hanging on crosses to rot, but Pilate granted this special favor. Joseph acted with great courage to give his Lord an honorable resting place.

Joseph took Jesus down from the cross, wrapped the body in clean linen cloth, and laid Him in a tomb cut into solid rock. This tomb had never been used before, so no other body had ever rested there. This unique tomb made it certain that only Jesus rose when the grave became empty.

These events happened late on Friday afternoon, which was the Preparation Day before the Sabbath. The Jewish Sabbath began at sundown, when lights were lit in homes for the holy rest. The burial had to be finished quickly before the work laws of the Sabbath began.

The faithful women who had followed Jesus from Galilee went along to watch the burial. They carefully noted exactly where the tomb was and how the body was placed inside the rock. Their love made sure they could find the exact spot when they returned.

The women hurried home to mix fragrant spices and sweet-smelling oils to place on Jesus' body. Then they stopped all work and rested on the Sabbath day to obey God's commandment. Their careful rest showed their deep respect for God's law, even in the middle of their great sadness.
